title: MVP-LAM: Learning Action-Centric Latent Action via Cross-Viewpoint Reconstruction
one_liner: Learn action representations from videos by forcing one camera view's action code to predict what happens next in a different camera view.
lead: When a robot learns to grasp from human videos, it needs to extract what the action actually is — not just memorize camera-specific details like lighting or angle. This paper shows how to train action representations that focus on the real movement and ignore viewpoint noise by asking one camera view to explain the future in a different camera view.

problem.h2: The viewpoint trap: actions tangled with camera angles
paras: When robots learn to grasp from human videos, they need to compress each action into a code — a small set of numbers. A naive approach: watch the frames and guess what action happened. But this breaks because the code soaks up camera-specific junk: sunlight from the left, the angle of the table, the person's height. Two videos of the identical grasp from different camera angles produce wildly different codes.

A beginner might try: collect videos from one camera angle and hope the code stays pure. This fails because real robot deployments see new angles, new lighting, new tables. The code learned from one view does not generalize.

callout.html: Action codes end up encoding camera angles and lighting instead of the real action, making them useless when the camera moves.

panels.title: 1. Two cameras, one grasp
panels.caption: Same hand grasp, filmed from left and right angles simultaneously.

panels.title: 2. Naive code: camera-specific junk
panels.caption: Left view code learns bright sunlight, table tilt, arm position.

panels.title: 3. Cross-view constraint: must explain both futures
panels.caption: Force left-view code to predict what the right camera sees next.

panels.title: 4. Code must strip camera junk
panels.caption: Sunlight and angles do not transfer; code must capture pure motion.

panels.title: 5. Action code works everywhere
panels.caption: Same grasp code predicts actions in new cameras, new lighting, new scenes.

steps.text: Film the same robot action or human task from two or more camera angles at once.
Train an encoder that reads left-camera frames and squashes them into a small action code.
Build a decoder that takes that action code and reconstructs what the right-camera will see next.
Measure how wrong the reconstruction is; tune the encoder and decoder to minimize error.
Because lighting and camera angle do not transfer between views, the code is forced to retain only real action.

object.h2: The one thing the paper changes
paras: The paper changes how action codes are learned. Instead of a single-view encoder that predicts actions from one camera, it builds a cross-view encoder: given frames from camera A, produce an action code that must reconstruct the future pixels in camera B.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: mutual information with ground-truth action
hidden.name: how much action the code retains
paras: The paper measures a hidden quantity: does the learned action code actually contain the ground-truth action, or just camera artifacts? The paper calls this mutual information — a number (in bits) that counts how much information the code shares with the true action, measured on held-out data.

The paper estimates this by asking: given the action code, how well can a separate predictor guess the true action label (grasp, pinch, push, etc.)? A higher score means the code absorbed the action; a low score means the code is full of camera noise. MVP-LAM's key claim: cross-viewpoint reconstruction training raises this score higher than single-view training.

heat.caption: Darker means more ground-truth action information. Cross-view codes (highlighted) contain more action, less camera junk.

reads.html: A good action code should let you guess the real task just by looking at it. Cross-view training makes that guess much easier.
Mutual information I(Code; Action) measures how many bits of true action live in the code. MVP-LAM achieves higher I than baselines.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the cross-view bottleneck
paras: The encoder reads left-camera frames and squeezes them into a tiny code. The decoder must then reconstruct what the right camera sees next, using only that code. Camera-specific junk — sunlight from the left, the table tilt in the left frame, the arm's position in the left camera's coordinates — does not transfer to the right camera, because the right camera has different lighting, a different viewing angle, and a different coordinate system. The decoder cannot use sunlight or angle to predict right-camera pixels; only the pure hand motion (gripper opening, reach direction, approach angle) appears in both views.

So the encoder is forced to discard camera junk and keep only the action. This is a bottleneck: the code is small (many details cannot fit), and the only details that pass through are the ones that appear in both views — the action itself. The decoder learns to take the action code and predict which pixels the right camera will see next, using the known camera angles and positions.

stages.s: Encoder squashes to small action code
Decoder reads code, knows right-camera angle and position
Minimize reconstruction error; code captures action only

math.words: Take the action code from camera A and try to reconstruct the pixels in camera B. The penalty is the sum of squared differences between predicted and actual pixels. Sum this over all pixel positions.
symbols: the total error the optimizer tries to shrink
what the decoder guesses the right camera will show
what the right camera actually showed in the video

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Say the right camera has 100 pixels and the prediction is off by 0.1 per pixel on average.
If a pixel is off by 0.2, that single pixel contributes 0.04, making the total 1.03.
The encoder learns to keep only information that reduces this pixel error across all 100 pixels and all frames.

math.note: The magic is that pixels only match if the code captures the true action motion, not camera-specific confounds.

charts.title: Naive single-view training
charts.note: Single-view code is mostly camera junk; task-specific action is buried.

items.html: The method requires recording the same action from multiple camera angles. Single-camera datasets cannot be used; this is a hard constraint.
If one camera view shows the hand but the other view has the hand hidden behind the table, reconstruction becomes impossible and the code must memorize the occlusion, not the action.
If the two cameras are not perfectly time-synchronized, frame A from the left camera does not match frame A from the right camera. Timestamp misalignment ruins the loss signal.

MVP-LAM works well when the dataset is consistent: similar lighting, similar robot or hand, similar tasks. It is less clear if one dataset of grasps and one dataset of pouring can be mixed; each may need separate training.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Record 10 seconds of a robot grasp from two mounted cameras. Train a simple encoder (e.g. a 3-layer convolutional neural network) using the cross-viewpoint objective: encode left-camera frames into a code of fixed size (e.g. 128 numbers), then train a decoder to reconstruct right-camera frames from that code alone. Log the reconstruction error as training progresses. Then freeze the encoder and test it on a new grasp task (a different object, a different hand position). Measure: on new data, how well does the code from camera A still reconstruct camera B? This should stay high if the code is action-centric and low if it is camera-specific.
demo.closing: The demo succeeds when the code trained on known grasps still reconstructs new grasps from the alternate camera, proving the code learned the action, not the camera.
